meta.description: Yes — it's the genuine opening line and refrain of Dylan Thomas's 1947 villanelle, first published 1951. Note: he wrote "gentle," not "gently."
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Do not go gentle into that good night'?
meta.ogDescription: The real, verified line from Dylan Thomas's villanelle (written 1947, published 1951) — and why "gently" is the world's favorite misquote of it.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This is the true opening line and recurring refrain of Thomas’s villanelle of the same name, written in 1947 and first published in the journal Botteghe Oscure in 1951. The wording is genuine — and note the adjective “gentle,” not the adverb “gently.”

source.excerpt:
Do not go gentle into that good night,
Old age should burn and rave at close of day;
Rage, rage against the dying of the light.
trail: Wikipedia’s article documents the poem as a villanelle by Dylan Thomas, written 1947 and first published in Botteghe Oscure in 1951.
The line is the poem’s title and opening refrain; the Academy of American Poets text shows the exact wording.
The poem was later collected in In Country Sleep, and Other Poems (New Directions, 1952) and Collected Poems, 1934–1952 (Dent, 1952), per Wikipedia.
source.excerptNote: The opening tercet. The first and third lines return as alternating refrains throughout the poem and close it as a couplet.

source.rightsNote: First published in 1951 — comfortably after the 1931 line — so in the United States this poem remains in copyright (US-published works from 1951 run 95 years from publication). Thomas died in 1953, and the poem entered the public domain in most life-plus-70 countries on 1 January 2024, but not in the US.

author.name: Dylan Thomas
author.heading: About Dylan Thomas
author.bio: Dylan Marlais Thomas (1914–1953) was a Welsh poet born in Swansea, celebrated for the musical intensity of his verse and his popular radio and stage work, including the “play for voices” Under Milk Wood. “Do not go gentle into that good night,” addressed to his ailing father, is his most quoted poem. He died in New York in 1953 at the age of 39.

misattribution.heading: The misquote everyone makes
misattribution.intro: The attribution here is not in doubt — the problem is the wording. The world’s favorite way to misquote this line is to “correct” Thomas’s grammar.

items.who: “Do not go gently into that good night”
items.why: Countless quotations swap Thomas’s adjective “gentle” for the adverb “gently.” Read as a predicate adjective, “gentle” describes the person (do not go gentle, i.e. meek) rather than merely the manner of going — so the swap changes the sense, not just the grammar. Thomas’s wording is “gentle,” as Wikipedia’s article on the poem confirms.

misattribution.truthLine: Thomas really wrote it — and he wrote “gentle,” not “gently.” Check the authoritative text.

context.heading: Why it endures
lead: Thomas wrote the villanelle in 1947, and it is widely read as a plea to his dying father to fight rather than surrender to death — though his father, D. J. Thomas, did not die until late 1952. The tight villanelle form, with its two hammering refrains, turns a private grief into a universal cry against mortality.
The poem has since saturated popular culture, from eulogies to films (memorably Interstellar), which is exactly why the slightly-off “gently” version circulates so widely.
context.pull: Rage, rage against the dying of the light.
